live_data_statements: Each participant completed trials requiring the identification of angry and happy facial expressions (emotion is a within-subject factor), and was randomly assigned to one of two independent groups via separate recruitment links, corresponding to two distinct intensity conditions (between-subject factor): the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions.
In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants were presented with either angry or happy facial expressions at a maximum yet not-equalized level of intensity.

Two independent cohorts of participants were recruited via the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/) through separate study links, with the target population being native of the USA and the UK.

Participants were also excluded if they identified as neurodiverse, reported ongoing mental health conditions or treatment, were taking psychotropic medication, or reported having been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit disorder, or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
In total, 259 participants were recruited: 134 in the unmatched-intensity condition and 125 in the matched-intensity condition.
After all criteria were applied, 14 participants were excluded from the unmatched-intensity condition, necessitating the recruitment of 10 additional individuals to achieve the target sample size.
Upon reapplying all exclusion criteria to the entire updated sample, 119 participants remained eligible, from which a random subsample of 115 was extracted for analysis.
In the matched-intensity condition, 6 participants were excluded following the application of the accuracy-based criterion, yielding a final eligible sample of 119.
To familiarize participants with the task logic, a visual analogy was provided: participants were shown a reference blue square and asked to estimate its brightness on a 1-6 scale.

Analogously, participants were asked to treat the happy expression as a reference point along an imagined intensity continuum and to select the corresponding anger frame that best matched this perceived intensity.
After all participants completed this intensity-matching task, we calculated the mean frame selection across all participants to identify the matched-intensity angry stimulus for the experiment.
Upon accessing the study link, participants were first presented with a comprehensive overview of the experimental procedures, including detailed information on data confidentiality and security.
Only individuals who explicitly provided informed consent were allowed to proceed with the task.
To ensure consistency in stimulus presentation and response modality, participants were instructed to complete the experiment on a laptop or desktop computer.

On each trial, participants were presented with an array of eight grayscale photographs of facial expressions arranged in a circular layout (Fig. 1), with each face having the same eccentricity with respect to a central fixation point.
Participants were instructed to indicate, as quickly and accurately as possible, whether an emotional facial expression was present or absent in the set by pressing designated keys.
Participants were required to respond to every trial for the experiment to proceed.
The estimated duration of the task was approximately 30 minutes, and compensation was provided at a rate of $8/hour, in accordance with Prolific's recommended payment guidelines.
Upon completing the task, participants were redirected to a debriefing page, which included a completion code to claim their compensation.
Recruitment was conducted using the "Include List" feature on the Prolific platform, which facilitated the precise identification and targeted re-invitation of eligible individuals.
The maximum data collection period was set at two weeks; however, data collection could conclude earlier if all eligible participants completed the task before the deadline.
As specified in the preregistration update, if fewer than 115 participants completed Study 2, additional participants with no prior involvement in any of our experiments would be recruited.
These new participants were asked to complete both the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions in that fixed order, separated by a washout period of at least two weeks.
No participants were excluded based on completion times below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR).

For this in-lab experiment we recruited a convenience sample of 16 participants (8 females; M age = 25 ± 3 years), who completed the standard visual search task involving angry and happy facial expressions across different experimental conditions.
Participants were adult Italian volunteers, recruited through local university channels and word-of-mouth.
After receiving a detailed explanation of the experimental procedures, all eligible participants provided written informed consent to take part in the study.
As in Study 1, participants were asked to perform an intensity-matching task through the designated web interface (see Fig. S1 in Supplementary Materials).
Trial types and spatial arrangements were randomized within each block.
Prior to the experimental task, participants completed the short form of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI-SF; [53]) to assess their dominant hand preference.
All participants were given a practice session of five trials to familiarize them with the procedure before starting the experiment.
Overall, each participant completed 200 trials (40 trials per 5 blocks), of which 80% contained one discrepant target and 20% did not.

Furthermore, participants were recruited online from the United States and the United Kingdom in Studies 1 and 2, and from Italy in Study 3, potentially limiting generalizability across cultural contexts.
No monetary compensation was offered, and participants were informed of their right to withdraw from the experiment at any time.

report: #### MATLAB code, no reproducible output

8 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run `diary('output.txt')` (or `diary on`) before the analysis and `diary off` after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use `publish('script.m', 'pdf')` (or the Live Editor's Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.

text.text: Humans are assumed to prioritize facial expressions because of the evolutionary significance of their affective content.
Here, we show that this assumption does not survive rigorous control of perceptual structure.

Across three studies integrating preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial expressions, and eye-tracking data, and combining frequentist interval testing with a predefined smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses, we tested whether detection advantages for happy and angry faces are better explained by the perceptual distinctiveness of stimuli than by their affective content.
Behavioral and oculomotor measures reliably predicted emotion category when expressions were presented at full, perceptually unbalanced, intensity.
By contrast, when expression intensity was matched, both interval testing and Bayesian ROPE analyses supported the absence of a practically meaningful effect.
In addition, detection speed and accuracy were best explained by geometric deviation from a neutral face, independent of emotional category.

These findings indicate that apparent emotion advantages in visual search arise from the perceptual characteristics of facial expressions rather than from privileged access to emotional meaning, challenging evolutionary accounts of attentional prioritization.
Humans are social beings whose successful functioning depends on efficiently interpreting others' mental states and preparing appropriate responses [1].
text.formatted: Humans are social beings whose successful functioning depends on efficiently interpreting others' mental states and preparing appropriate responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Because attentional resources are limited, perceptual systems are thought to prioritize cues that signal affective and socially relevant information over competing input.
From an evolutionary perspective, such prioritization is assumed to confer adaptive advantages by facilitating rapid responses to emotionally significant stimuli [2, 3].
text.formatted: From an evolutionary perspective, such prioritization is assumed to confer adaptive advantages by facilitating rapid responses to emotionally significant stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3]</ref>.

text.text: Although facial expressions do not map one-to-one onto subjective emotional experience [4], the human face remains a powerful tool to signal social intentions.
text.formatted: Although facial expressions do not map one-to-one onto subjective emotional experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, the human face remains a powerful tool to signal social intentions.

text.text: Smiles, for example, often signal affiliation, whereas baring the teeth can signal threat [5].
text.formatted: Smiles, for example, often signal affiliation, whereas baring the teeth can signal threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with their social relevance, numerous studies report facilitated detection of emotional relative to neutral faces (e.g., [6] [7] [8]), an effect commonly interpreted as reflecting adaptive prioritization.
text.formatted: Consistent with their social relevance, numerous studies report facilitated detection of emotional relative to neutral faces (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>), an effect commonly interpreted as reflecting adaptive prioritization.

text.text: Importantly, this attentional preference has been observed even when emotional expressions were irrelevant to the task, for example with both happy and angry faces attracting the gaze during visual search even though the target was defined by gender [9].
text.formatted: Importantly, this attentional preference has been observed even when emotional expressions were irrelevant to the task, for example with both happy and angry faces attracting the gaze during visual search even though the target was defined by gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: This raises a critical question: Are all facial expressions prioritized equally, or do specific expressions, such as threat-related versus affiliative signals, receive preferential access to attention?

One influential account holds that stimuli signaling potential threat receive prioritized access to attentional resources because their rapid detection supports timely fight-or-flight responses (the threat-advantage hypothesis; [10, 11]).
text.formatted: One influential account holds that stimuli signaling potential threat receive prioritized access to attentional resources because their rapid detection supports timely fight-or-flight responses (the threat-advantage hypothesis; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>).

text.text: This view predicts the "face-in-the-crowd" effect: Angry faces should be detected more efficiently than non-threatening faces because of their hostile value.

Empirical support for this claim largely comes from visual search studies reporting faster and more accurate detection of angry faces among neutral distractors [12] [13] [14], with performance interpreted as a proxy for emotion-driven attentional prioritization.
text.formatted: Empirical support for this claim largely comes from visual search studies reporting faster and more accurate detection of angry faces among neutral distractors <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, with performance interpreted as a proxy for emotion-driven attentional prioritization.

text.text: Subsequent work challenged the threat-advantage account by showing that prioritization effects for angry faces were confounded by low-level visual properties of the stimuli [15].
text.formatted: Subsequent work challenged the threat-advantage account by showing that prioritization effects for angry faces were confounded by low-level visual properties of the stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: In response, researchers adopted schematic faces, which allow geometric features to be manipulated while ostensibly controlling low-level visual characteristics.

Although detection advantages for negatively valenced expressions were frequently replicated using such stimuli [13, 16], their interpretation proved inconsistent, as schematic features often failed to map onto specific emotional categories [12, 17].
text.formatted: Although detection advantages for negatively valenced expressions were frequently replicated using such stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>, their interpretation proved inconsistent, as schematic features often failed to map onto specific emotional categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: More strikingly, Horstmann and colleagues [18] demonstrated that modifying the geometry of the facial outline could reverse the direction of the search asymmetry without substantially altering the perceived emotional valence of the faces.
text.formatted: More strikingly, Horstmann and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> demonstrated that modifying the geometry of the facial outline could reverse the direction of the search asymmetry without substantially altering the perceived emotional valence of the faces.

text.text: In addition, other studies failed to replicate an anger superiority effect (ASE [10]; e.g., [15, 19]), and have often reported the existence of a happiness superiority effect (HSE; [20]).
text.formatted: In addition, other studies failed to replicate an anger superiority effect (ASE <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>), and have often reported the existence of a happiness superiority effect (HSE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>).

text.text: In HSE, happy faces are detected more rapidly and accurately than angry or fearful faces among neutral distractors [8, [21] [22], an advantage that is especially pronounced when photographic images of real faces are used [23].
text.formatted: In HSE, happy faces are detected more rapidly and accurately than angry or fearful faces among neutral distractors <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>, an advantage that is especially pronounced when photographic images of real faces are used <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: However, both ASE and HSE have been reported with photographic faces depending on the stimulus set employed [24], and subsequent work has shown that changing even a few facial identities within the same database can reverse the direction of the reaction-time advantage [25].
text.formatted: However, both ASE and HSE have been reported with photographic faces depending on the stimulus set employed <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>, and subsequent work has shown that changing even a few facial identities within the same database can reverse the direction of the reaction-time advantage <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Öhman and coauthors [26] likewise demonstrated that distractor redundancy and target gender affected the relative prioritization of angry versus happy faces, with an anger superiority effect emerging specifically for male targets among redundant distractors.
text.formatted: Öhman and coauthors <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> likewise demonstrated that distractor redundancy and target gender affected the relative prioritization of angry versus happy faces, with an anger superiority effect emerging specifically for male targets among redundant distractors.

text.text: Given the inconsistent pattern of detection advantages observed across studies, it is reasonable to question whether these effects reflect emotion at all.

An alternative explanation comes from computational models of visual salience, which propose that selective attention can be guided by local variations in basic image properties, such as luminance, contrast and edge orientation [27] [28].
text.formatted: An alternative explanation comes from computational models of visual salience, which propose that selective attention can be guided by local variations in basic image properties, such as luminance, contrast and edge orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Applied to facial expressions, this account suggests that detection advantages may arise from the perceptual distinctiveness of specific facial features rather than from their emotional meaning [29].
text.formatted: Applied to facial expressions, this account suggests that detection advantages may arise from the perceptual distinctiveness of specific facial features rather than from their emotional meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: For instance, Horstmann and colleagues [30] demonstrated that mouth opening and the accompanying visibility of teeth may facilitate visual search for both happy and angry faces, potentially producing a superiority effect for either expression.
text.formatted: For instance, Horstmann and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> demonstrated that mouth opening and the accompanying visibility of teeth may facilitate visual search for both happy and angry faces, potentially producing a superiority effect for either expression.

text.text: The contribution of such features has also been investigated by disrupting normal face processing through scrambling or inversion, while leaving local visual information available.
Search efficiency remained largely unaffected by face inversion [31] and both anger and happiness superiority effects were observed in this context [32].
text.formatted: Search efficiency remained largely unaffected by face inversion <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> and both anger and happiness superiority effects were observed in this context <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Building on this literature, we conducted a rigorous comparison of ASE and HSE by systematically varying the degree of perceptual distinctiveness between angry and happy photographic faces to test whether detection advantages for either emotion persist once expressionrelated perceptual differences are minimized.

To this aim, we extracted static frames from dynamic facial expressions of happiness and anger [33] at two intensity levels: a maximal, perceptually unmatched, intensity and an intermediate, perceptually matched, intensity.
text.formatted: To this aim, we extracted static frames from dynamic facial expressions of happiness and anger <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> at two intensity levels: a maximal, perceptually unmatched, intensity and an intermediate, perceptually matched, intensity.

text.text: Participants performed a visual search task in which they identified a single happy or angry face among neutral distractors.
This manipulation allowed us to test whether shorter detection times and higher accuracy for one emotion persist when lower-level perceptual structure is controlled.
If detection advantages reflect privileged access to affective meaning, a consistent advantage for specific expressions should emerge in both matched and unmatched conditions.

Conversely, if attentional prioritization is driven by the perceptual characteristics of the stimuli, an advantage should arise only when expressions differ in these characteristics and should disappear once intensity and magnitude of facial displacement are equated between emotions.

We tested these competing predictions across three studies combining preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial stimuli, and eye-tracking data to assess both detection performance and attentional dynamics.

We then used interval testing and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses to formally assess competing hypotheses (i.e., presence or absence of an emotion-driven performance advantage).

Results converged on a perceptual account: detection performance differed between emotions only under the perceptually unmatched condition, where affective meaning covaried with perceptual distinctiveness.
This asymmetry disappeared when perceptual features were matched across emotion categories, thereby dissociating emotion from differences in stimulus appearance.

Oculomotor behavior likewise varied more between emotions in the unmatched than in the matched condition, both in the time taken to first look at a face (time to first fixation) and the total time spent looking at it (dwell time), suggesting a faster visual search only when perceptual distinctiveness is maximal.
Last, behavioral performance correlated with the geometric displacement of the emotional facial expressions from neutrality.
A 2×2 mixed-design experimental paradigm was employed to examine participants' performance in a visual search task involving the detection of emotional facial expressions.

Each participant completed trials requiring the identification of angry and happy facial expressions (emotion is a within-subject factor), and was randomly assigned to one of two independent groups via separate recruitment links, corresponding to two distinct intensity conditions (between-subject factor): the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions.
In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants were presented with either angry or happy facial expressions at a maximum yet not-equalized level of intensity.

Within this context, we anticipated a detection advantage for happy faces, grounded in existing literature suggesting that in photographic stimuli uncorrected low-level visual features (most notably, the pronounced luminance and contrast associated with a conspicuous, tooth-exposing smile) may enhance perceptual distinctiveness and facilitate detection [34].
text.formatted: Within this context, we anticipated a detection advantage for happy faces, grounded in existing literature suggesting that in photographic stimuli uncorrected low-level visual features (most notably, the pronounced luminance and contrast associated with a conspicuous, tooth-exposing smile) may enhance perceptual distinctiveness and facilitate detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we use the term "perceptual distinctiveness" to refer to the visual characteristics of facial expressions that influence their detection during visual search.
These characteristics can affect performance through the interplay of bottom-up (e.g., feature contrast) and top-down mechanisms (e.g., goal-directed attentional guidance).

By contrast, the matched-intensity condition employed stimuli at an intermediate level of intensity, perceptually-equalized across emotions to minimize differences in low-level visual features (see Stimulus selection and perceptual matching for details).
We hypothesized that correcting for such perceptual confounds would eliminate the detection bias observed in the unmatched-intensity condition.

In both conditions, visual search performance was assessed through two behavioral metrics: response accuracy (i.e., correct identification of the presence or absence of an emotional target among neutral distractors) and reaction time (i.e., latency between stimulus onset to keypress response).

Our study intended to test two complementary hypotheses: first, that a practical and statistical difference exists in the detection of happy versus angry faces when stimuli are unbalanced in terms of low-level visual features (i.e., the unmatched-intensity condition); and second, that such a practical and statistical difference would no longer be observed when perceptual features are matched between emotions (i.e., the matched-intensity condition).
Demonstrating both the presence and absence of an effect necessitates an analytical approach capable of supporting inferences in both directions.
Conventional Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) is not suitable for this purpose [35].
text.formatted: Conventional Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) is not suitable for this purpose <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, traditional NHST can provide evidence against the null hypothesis (H 0 ) when p-values fall below a predetermined threshold (e.g., p < .05), but it cannot support H 0 when results are statistically non-significant.
text.formatted: Specifically, traditional NHST can provide evidence against the null hypothesis (H 0 ) when p-values fall below a predetermined threshold (e.g., p < .05), but it cannot support H 0 when results are statistically non-significant.

text.text: To overcome this limitation, we adopted an interval testing approach, which enables inferences about the presence or the absence of an effect by comparing the observed statistics and its 95% confidence interval to a predefined threshold of practical significance [36].
text.formatted: To overcome this limitation, we adopted an interval testing approach, which enables inferences about the presence or the absence of an effect by comparing the observed statistics and its 95% confidence interval to a predefined threshold of practical significance <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>.

text.text: This threshold, known as the Smallest Effect Size of Interest or SESOI, represents the minimum effect size deemed practical for interpretation.
If the entire 95% confidence interval (CI) lies above the SESOI threshold, the result is interpreted as supportive of the alternative hypothesis (H 1 ), indicating a practically meaningful effect.
Conversely, if the CI lies entirely below the SESOI, the result supports the null hypothesis (H 0 ), suggesting the absence of such an effect.
If the CI overlaps the SESOI, the result is considered inconclusive.

To determine the sample size needed to achieve at least 80% statistical power under the interval testing framework, we conducted a simulation-based power analysis using pilot data (n = 52) from the unmatched-intensity condition [37].
text.formatted: To determine the sample size needed to achieve at least 80% statistical power under the interval testing framework, we conducted a simulation-based power analysis using pilot data (n = 52) from the unmatched-intensity condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: All parameters and procedures described in the following section were specified a priori in our preregistration (see http://osf.io/sjvak).

text.text: In pilot data, a machine learning classifier was able to predict whether the stimulus was a happy or angry face based on participants' task performance, achieving a classification accuracy of 70%, with a bootstrapped 95% confidence interval (CI) of [67%, 73%].

Given that effect sizes derived from small samples are typically inflated [38] [39], we adopted a more conservative estimate of 68% (closer to the lower bound of the CI) for the true population accuracy and simulated 10,000 experiments, each drawing a random sample of participants ranging between 26 and 180, with each participant completing 190 trials of the visual search task (95 trials with happy faces and 95 with angry faces).
text.formatted: Given that effect sizes derived from small samples are typically inflated <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>, we adopted a more conservative estimate of 68% (closer to the lower bound of the CI) for the true population accuracy and simulated 10,000 experiments, each drawing a random sample of participants ranging between 26 and 180, with each participant completing 190 trials of the visual search task (95 trials with happy faces and 95 with angry faces).

text.text: The threshold for practical significance was set at 66%.

Because model performance would be evaluated using a 60%-20%-20% train-validationtest split to obtain an unbiased estimate of cross-validated accuracy, the number of trials in the test set ranged from 988 (n = 26) to 6,840 (n = 180).

For each simulated test set, we calculated the 95% confidence interval of classification accuracy and interpreted the outcome as supporting H 1 , H 0 , or inconclusive result, depending on whether the interval lay entirely above, entirely below, or overlapped the SESOI, respectively.
Results indicated that with 115 participants, corresponding to 4,370 trials in the test set, H 0 would be rejected in 81% of simulations, which corresponds to 81% statistical power for H 1 .
The same sample size was targeted for the matched-intensity condition in the between-subject design.

Two independent cohorts of participants were recruited via the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/) through separate study links, with the target population being native of the USA and the UK.
text.formatted: Two independent cohorts of participants were recruited via the Prolific platform (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.com/">https://www.prolific.com/</ref>) through separate study links, with the target population being native of the USA and the UK.

text.text: Recruitment settings were configured to ensure that participants who completed one condition were excluded from participating in the other, thereby maintaining the independence of the two groups.
The current study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and received formal approval from the local Ethics Committee (Protocol No.
12/2022, "Comitato Etico Congiunto per la ricerca della Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna e della Scuola Normale Superiore").

All data were collected anonymously and handled in strict accordance with current data protection legislation, including the Italian Legislative Decree 196/2003 and the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (EU GDPR 679/2016).
No personally identifiable information was gathered, and the data were used exclusively for scientific and statistical purposes.
All participants retained the right to withdraw from the study at any time without any consequences by simply closing the browser window.
Exclusion criteria included self-reported history of mental illness, language-related disorders, or head injury.

Participants were also excluded if they identified as neurodiverse, reported ongoing mental health conditions or treatment, were taking psychotropic medication, or reported having been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit disorder, or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
In total, 259 participants were recruited: 134 in the unmatched-intensity condition and 125 in the matched-intensity condition.

To account for potential participant exclusion based on our preregistered criteria (see OSF Registration, Data Exclusion section), we intentionally over-recruited beyond the minimum required sample size, ensuring that each condition retained a sufficiently powered sample of 115 participants after data cleaning.
Recruitment was initially capped at 250 participants (125 per group).

If more than 115 eligible participants per group provided usable data, a random subsample of 115 was selected; if fewer met the criteria, recruitment was extended until the target sample size was reached.
Data were excluded based on two levels: participant and trial.
At the participant level, we evaluated total task completion time and response accuracy.

Here, completion time refers to the total amount of time elapsed from when a participant clicks on the study link to when they submit their final response and are redirected to the debriefing page (see Experimental procedure for details).

Participants with completion times falling below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) were flagged for exclusion, as short durations may indicate insufficient engagement with the task.
However, no participants met this criterion.
Accuracy-based exclusions were applied separately for each emotion category.
Participants whose accuracy scores in either category fell below Q1 -1.5 × IQR were excluded to minimize the impact of random responding, inattentiveness, or misunderstanding of task instructions.
No upper threshold was set for accuracy, as high performance was interpreted as evidence of appropriate task engagement.
At the single-trial level, exclusions were based on reaction times (RTs).
Trials with RTs exceeding the third quartile (Q3) plus 1.5 × IQR were removed, as excessively long latencies may reflect distraction or disengagement.
After all criteria were applied, 14 participants were excluded from the unmatched-intensity condition, necessitating the recruitment of 10 additional individuals to achieve the target sample size.
Upon reapplying all exclusion criteria to the entire updated sample, 119 participants remained eligible, from which a random subsample of 115 was extracted for analysis.
At the trial level, 1,110 trials were excluded due to excessively long response times.
In the matched-intensity condition, 6 participants were excluded following the application of the accuracy-based criterion, yielding a final eligible sample of 119.
As this number met the pre-specified minimal threshold, no further recruitment was required.
A random subsample of 115 participants was again selected for analysis, and 1,320 trials were excluded on the basis of delayed response times.

Unlike many facial expression datasets that rely on static or artificially generated stimuli, we constructed our stimulus set using the "Amsterdam Dynamic Facial Expression Set" (ADFES), a validated database comprising 648 dynamic emotional expressions performed by 22 professional actors (10 female, 12 male) from diverse ethnic backgrounds.
The use of real actors is essential for eliciting affective responses in viewers [40].
text.formatted: The use of real actors is essential for eliciting affective responses in viewers <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>.

text.text: ADFES includes portrayals of nine discrete emotions: the six Ekman's basic ones (anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise) alongside contempt, pride and embarrassment.
Each video has a duration of approximately 6 to 6.5 seconds, beginning with a 500-millisecond neutral baseline, followed by the onset of the expression, and culminating in a 5-second apex phase.

Emotional expressions were generated using standardized configurations of facial Action Units (AUs), incorporating the most characteristic features outlined by Ekman and Friesen [41], Keltner [42], and Tracy & Robins [43].
text.formatted: Emotional expressions were generated using standardized configurations of facial Action Units (AUs), incorporating the most characteristic features outlined by <ref type="bibr">Ekman and</ref> Friesen <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>, Keltner <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>, and Tracy & Robins <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref>.

text.text: The ADFES stimuli have been extensively validated and received excellent recognition rates [33].
text.formatted: The ADFES stimuli have been extensively validated and received excellent recognition rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: For the purposes of this study, only video clips depicting anger and happiness were selected.

To identify peak-intensity frames for the unmatched-intensity condition, we computed the displacement fields aligning two temporally consecutive frames from each video sequence using the imregdemons function in MATLAB [44].
text.formatted: To identify peak-intensity frames for the unmatched-intensity condition, we computed the displacement fields aligning two temporally consecutive frames from each video sequence using the imregdemons function in MATLAB <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>.

text.text: This image registration technique enabled us to detect the frame with the highest value of framewise displacement, which corresponds to the apex of the expression.
The procedure was applied to both happy and angry clips for a selected subset of actors (n = 19).
These selected frames served as experimental stimuli in the unmatchedintensity condition.

We assessed the perceptual validity of this displacement-based selection by collecting independent intensity judgments from human scorers (n = 9; 6 females, M age = 33 ± 7 years) and comparing their choices with the frames identified by the registration algorithm.

In this validation task, participants viewed all frames from the anger and happiness sequences and, for each actor, selected the frame they perceived as displaying the highest level of expressive intensity.

To quantify the geometric similarity between the frames selected by human observers and those identified by the displacement-based procedure, we reconstructed the 3D facial geometry of each frame using Medusa (Schyns Lab; https://schynslab.github.io/medusa), a Python-based toolbox for dynamic face modeling [45] [46] [47].
text.formatted: To quantify the geometric similarity between the frames selected by human observers and those identified by the displacement-based procedure, we reconstructed the 3D facial geometry of each frame using Medusa (Schyns Lab; <ref type="url" target="https://schynslab.github.io/medusa">https://schynslab.github.io/medusa</ref>), a Python-based toolbox for dynamic face modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref>.

text.text: For each video stimulus, a three-dimensional tensor of vertex coordinates (3 × 468 × 150) was generated, corresponding to the x, y, and z spatial positions of 468 tracked facial landmarks across 150 frames.
For each actor, the human-selected and displacement-based meshes were then compared by computing the root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) between corresponding vertices (see [48] for details).
text.formatted: For each actor, the human-selected and displacement-based meshes were then compared by computing the root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) between corresponding vertices (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref> for details).

text.text: Vertex-wise Euclidean distances were first obtained for all 468 points, squared, averaged, and square-rooted to yield a single RMSD value per pair.
This measure reflects the overall magnitude of geometric displacement between the two expressions and provides a standard index of facial shape difference [49] [50].
text.formatted: This measure reflects the overall magnitude of geometric displacement between the two expressions and provides a standard index of facial shape difference <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>.

text.text: To allow comparisons across actors with different facial scales, RMSD values were normalized by each actor's full range of facial deformation.

Normalized RMSD values were consistently small, well below 1% of the actor's total expressive motion range, indicating that participants' selections closely approximated the apex frames identified by the registration procedure.

A visualization of the two overlaid meshes (one obtained from the frame selected by the algorithm and one from the frame identified by human scorers) for each actor is provided in the Supplementary Materials.
For the matched-intensity condition, a two-stage selection process was employed.
First, video clips depicting happiness were manually inspected by one of the authors (E.B.) to identify the frame immediately preceding the exposure of teeth.
This step sought to minimize potential visual confounds, as exposed teeth may generate a "blob" of increased local contrast and luminance in the mouth region [34].
text.formatted: This step sought to minimize potential visual confounds, as exposed teeth may generate a "blob" of increased local contrast and luminance in the mouth region <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: After identifying happy facial expressions of intermediate intensity, an independent cohort of 11 scorers (7 females, M age = 31 ± 7 years) was recruited to perform an online intensity-matching task.
This cohort included all the scorers who participated in the selection of frames with maximum facial displacement and two additional participants.
Specifically, they were shown the pre-selected happy facial expression on the left side of the screen, serving as the reference stimulus.
On the right side, they could browse a sequence of static frames extracted from the anger video clips of the same actor or actress.
These frames were displayed in their original temporal order, progressing from a neutral expression to peak emotional intensity.

Using a slider, participants navigated through the entire sequence of the anger expression and were asked to select the frame they perceived as most closely matching the reference happy expression in terms of intensity (see Supplementary Materials, Fig. S1).
text.formatted: Using a slider, participants navigated through the entire sequence of the anger expression and were asked to select the frame they perceived as most closely matching the reference happy expression in terms of intensity (see Supplementary Materials, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">S1</ref>).

text.text: To familiarize participants with the task logic, a visual analogy was provided: participants were shown a reference blue square and asked to estimate its brightness on a 1-6 scale.
Subsequently, they viewed a series of green squares with varying brightness levels and were instructed to identify the one whose brightness most closely resembled that of the blue square.

Analogously, participants were asked to treat the happy expression as a reference point along an imagined intensity continuum and to select the corresponding anger frame that best matched this perceived intensity.
After all participants completed this intensity-matching task, we calculated the mean frame selection across all participants to identify the matched-intensity angry stimulus for the experiment.

This process resulted in the creation of 19 perceptually-equalized stimulus pairs, each consisting of one happy expression and one angry expression for each actor/actress, matched in terms of perceived emotional intensity.
These pairs were subsequently presented in the matchedintensity experimental condition.
Notably, all images underwent the same preprocessing pipeline.
Non-facial areas (e.g., hair, neck, etc.) were removed by applying a standardized ellipsoidal mask.

Images were then resized to equal dimensions, converted to grayscale, and normalized for luminance and spatial frequency using the SHINE toolbox for MATLAB [51], thereby ensuring parity in low-level visual properties across stimuli and conditions.
text.formatted: Images were then resized to equal dimensions, converted to grayscale, and normalized for luminance and spatial frequency using the SHINE toolbox for MATLAB <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref>, thereby ensuring parity in low-level visual properties across stimuli and conditions.

text.text: As a final step, we quantified geometric differences between stimulus pairs to assess how the facial configuration of angry and happy expressions varied across intensity conditions.

This analysis served to validate the intensity manipulation, with greater dissimilarity expected in the unmatched-intensity condition (where expressions were presented at maximal, unequalized intensity across emotions) and smaller dissimilarity anticipated in the matched-intensity condition, where expressions were intended to exhibit comparable perceptual distinctiveness.
Facial motion data were reconstructed using Medusa and geometric differences were computed using the same RMSD-based approach described above.
For each actor, the angry and happy target frames were compared to obtain a single RMSD value reflecting the magnitude of facial shape difference between the two expressions.

All RMSD values from the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions were subsequently compared using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test to assess whether intensity equalization significantly reduced the geometric disparity between angry and happy faces.

The experiment was conducted online and implemented through jsPsych [52], an opensource JavaScript library specifically designed for precise stimulus presentation and accurate behavioral data acquisition in web-based cognitive tasks.
text.formatted: The experiment was conducted online and implemented through jsPsych <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref>, an opensource JavaScript library specifically designed for precise stimulus presentation and accurate behavioral data acquisition in web-based cognitive tasks.

text.text: Upon accessing the study link, participants were first presented with a comprehensive overview of the experimental procedures, including detailed information on data confidentiality and security.
Only individuals who explicitly provided informed consent were allowed to proceed with the task.

Prior to the main experimental task, the short form of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI-SF; [53]), an abbreviated version of the original instrument developed by Oldfield [54], was administered to assess dominant hand preference and account for potential variability in task performance related to handedness.
text.formatted: Prior to the main experimental task, the short form of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (EHI-SF; <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref>), an abbreviated version of the original instrument developed by Oldfield <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref>, was administered to assess dominant hand preference and account for potential variability in task performance related to handedness.

text.text: To ensure consistency in stimulus presentation and response modality, participants were instructed to complete the experiment on a laptop or desktop computer.
The task comprised five blocks of 50 trials each, resulting in a total of 250 trials per participant.

On each trial, participants were presented with an array of eight grayscale photographs of facial expressions arranged in a circular layout (Fig. 1), with each face having the same eccentricity with respect to a central fixation point.
text.formatted: On each trial, participants were presented with an array of eight grayscale photographs of facial expressions arranged in a circular layout (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), with each face having the same eccentricity with respect to a central fixation point.

text.text: Arrays contained either exclusively neutral faces or a single emotionally-discrepant face (either angry or happy) among neutral distractors.

Therefore, the task was articulated into three trial types: (i) neutral arrays with no emotional face (60 trials total, 12 per block); (ii) arrays containing one angry face among neutral distractors (95 trials total, 19 per block); and (iii) arrays containing one happy face among neutral distractors (95 trials total, 19 per block).

Randomization was implemented at multiple levels to minimize systematic biases: (i) the sequence of trial types was randomized within each block of 50 trials, and (ii) stimulus location was randomized at the trial level by randomly assigning the actors to the eight possible locations on each trial.
However, to control for potential location-based confounds, each emotional expression (angry or happy) of a given actor was consistently assigned to the same location within a block.

For example, if an actor's angry expression appeared in Position 3 (e.g., north-east) in a given block, their happy expression was also presented in Position 3 during that block, ensuring that differences in detection accuracy or response times between emotions were not attributable to spatial location.
Participants were instructed to indicate, as quickly and accurately as possible, whether an emotional facial expression was present or absent in the set by pressing designated keys.
The online platform was designed to automatically record two primary trial-by-trial metrics throughout the experiment: detection accuracy and speed.
Accuracy was defined as the participant's correct identification of the presence/absence of an emotional expression among neutral distractors.

Speed was operationalized as reaction time (RT) measured in milliseconds (ms), and refers to the time interval between the presentation of the facial stimulus array on the screen and the participant's keypress response.
Participants were required to respond to every trial for the experiment to proceed.
The estimated duration of the task was approximately 30 minutes, and compensation was provided at a rate of $8/hour, in accordance with Prolific's recommended payment guidelines.
Upon completing the task, participants were redirected to a debriefing page, which included a completion code to claim their compensation.

To overcome limitations of traditional Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), which cannot provide support for the null hypothesis (H 0 ) when results are non-significant, we adopted an interval testing framework.

This involves specifying an acceptance region for H 0 and determining whether the observed effect falls within this region (supporting H 0 ) or outside it (supporting the alternative hypothesis, H 1 ).

This framework allowed for the formal evaluation of our hypotheses: (1) the presence of a difference in the detection of angry versus happy faces in the unmatched-intensity condition, and (2) the absence of such a difference in the matched-intensity condition.
We preregistered and developed a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification model to assess whether emotion category ("angry" vs. "happy") could be predicted from participants' task performance.

Input features included binary accuracy scores (1 = correct,0 = incorrect) and reaction times (RTs), which were normalized for each participant by subtracting the mean reaction time across conditions from individual trials, so as to account for differences in baseline response speed between individuals.
The target variable, or the outcome being predicted, was the emotion label associated with each trial.
To assess the predictive performance of our model, we employed a nested 5-Fold cross-validation procedure.
Thus, the dataset was first divided into five folds for outer cross-validation.
In each iteration, one fold was held out as a test set and the remaining four were used for learning.

Within each outer learning set, an additional inner 4-fold cross-validation (3 folds iteratively assigned to the training and 1 to the validation sets) was performed to identify the optimal number of neighbors (k) for the k-NN algorithm.
A range of k-values was tested, and the optimal k was chosen based on the smallest validation error across the inner folds.
The final k-NN model was trained on the entire outer learning set using the optimal k and evaluated on the held-out outer test fold.
This procedure was repeated across all outer folds, and classification accuracy (i.e., the proportion of correctly predicted trials) was computed for each one.
Bootstrapping of individual trials in the test set (10,000 resamples) was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals around the classification accuracy estimates.

Decision thresholds for H 0 and H 1 were preregistered before collection of any data and established using a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of 66% accuracy, which we considered practically significant for our analysis.

A bootstrapped confidence interval lying entirely above 66% was interpreted as support for H 1 , indicating that the behavioral predictors (speed and accuracy) reliably discriminate between angry and happy expressions.
Conversely, an interval entirely below 66% was interpreted as support for H 0 , suggesting that the behavioral features lack sufficient predictive value.
Confidence intervals overlapping the 66% threshold were deemed inconclusive.

To quantify the unique contribution of each behavioral predictor (i.e., response accuracy and detection speed) to the classifier's performance, we employed a permutation-based featureimportance analysis embedded within the outer loop of our nested cross-validation procedure.

After selecting the optimal number of neighbors (k) via the inner folds and computing the baseline test accuracy on the held-out data, we permuted the values of one feature within the training data, leaving all other features and the test set unchanged.
The classification accuracy of the permuted model was then evaluated on the test set, allowing us to measure the drop in accuracy attributable solely to the disruption of that feature's information.

The entire procedure was repeated 100 times per predictor and outer fold, yielding a distribution of permuted accuracies whose average deviation from the baseline provided an estimate of the feature's importance.
These scores were averaged across all five outer folds.
Large drops in accuracy indicated that the feature carried critical discriminative power, whereas minimal changes revealed a negligible role in distinguishing angry from happy expressions.

Although our primary inferences were based on comparing classification accuracy against a predefined practical threshold (SESOI = 66%) using a frequentist approach, we additionally conducted Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses [55] [56] for each emotion (angry, happy) and condition (matched, unmatched) to evaluate whether the data supported the absence of a practically meaningful advantage when facial displacement was equated across emotions.

text.text: We specified a uniform prior, Beta(1, 1), and leveraged the conjugacy of the beta distribution for proportions to compute the posterior in closed form.
Specifically, the a parameter was updated with the number of correctly classified trials and the b parameter with the number of misclassified trials.
This procedure was repeated for each outer fold of the k-Nearest Neighbors classifier.

Given the large number of observations per fold (i.e., thousands of trials), the likelihood was expected to dominate the posterior; consequently, although alternative prior specifications were not formally tested, the results are unlikely to be sensitive to the choice of prior.

Before assessing the k-NN performance in the unmatched-and matched-intensity groups, we verified that the two cohorts were demographically similar, ruling out potential confounds in age, gender, or handedness that might influence task performance.
To this end, we conducted several statistical controls.

Gender distributions were compared using Fisher's exact test, while group differences in age and laterality quotient (LQ), a continuous index of handedness retrieved from the administration of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, were assessed via two separate Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.

Also, to examine any gender-handedness interaction, LQs were binned into "left-handers", "ambidextrous", and "right-handers" categories, and gender-by-handedness frequencies cross-tabulated in separate 2×3 tables for each cohort.
Chi-squared test was used on each table to determine whether the observed distribution of handedness categories differed by gender more than expected by chance.

To further assess the potential influence of individual differences on classification performance, we conducted an additional non-preregistered k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) analysis in which demographic variables, namely gender, age, and laterality quotient, were incorporated into the feature set alongside behavioral measures of accuracy and response times.
Separate models were trained for the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions.
This procedure served as a robustness check to ensure that effects attributed to the experimental manipulation were not confounded by heterogeneity in demographics between groups.

If classification performance remained stable with the inclusion of these covariates, it would strengthen the interpretation that the observed effects primarily reflect task-related behavioral differences.
Feature importance scores were also computed to quantify the relative contributions of demographic and behavioral variables, replicating the analysis framework used for the preregistered analysis.

Nevertheless, to further control for inter-individual variability, we conducted a second experiment (Study 2) employing a within-subject design, thereby providing a stringent test of whether classification accuracy reflected stimulus properties rather than participant-level differences.

Beyond these group-level analyses, which involved training classifiers on pooled data across participants, we conducted a complementary non-preregistered single-subject k-NN approach to test whether each individual's behavioral responses could reliably discriminate between emotional expressions.
Specifically, we applied k-NN classification separately to each participant's data in both the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions.

For each of the 115 participants, trials involving happy and angry target expressions were selected, and a twodimensional feature space was constructed using range-normalized reaction times and binary accuracy values.

Within each participant's dataset, 20% of the trials were randomly held out as a test set, while the remaining 80% were partitioned into a training set and a 25% hold-out validation set to determine the optimal number of neighbors (k) by minimizing classification error.
The optimal k was then applied to the withheld test set, yielding a single accuracy score per participant.

To estimate the overall classification performance, we generated 10,000 bootstrap resamples of these individual accuracy scores and computed the mean test accuracy along with the corresponding 95% confidence interval for each condition.

In addition to our primary and preregistered k-NN classification and interval testing pipeline, we conducted additional exploratory analyses using Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMMs) to examine the effects of emotion and intensity condition on detection performance, while also accounting for participant-level and stimulus-level variability.
Response accuracy was modeled with a binomial distribution and logit link:

The fixed effects in this model included the main effects of emotion (either being presented with an angry or happy face among neutral distractors), experimental condition (unmatched vs. matched intensity), and their interaction, along with random intercepts for participant (participant_id), actor portraying the emotional expression (actor_id), and participant's laterality quotient (lq).
Participant and actor identities were incorporated to control for participant-specific and stimulusspecific baseline variability in performance, respectively.

The laterality quotient, derived from the administration of the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, was also included as a random effect to model any consistent influence of handedness-related factors on performance.

Consistent with our hypotheses, we expected a significant emotion × condition interaction, whereby the detection advantage for happy faces, likely attributable to the visual salience of the smile, would be pronounced in the unmatched-intensity condition and near-zero when expression intensity was perceptually equated across emotions.

For the reaction time analysis, we applied a similar modeling structure, this time leveraging an inverse Gaussian distribution with a log link to accommodate the positively skewed distribution of response times [61].

As with accuracy, we expected a significant emotion × condition interaction, reflecting a detection advantage for happy faces in the unmatched condition compared to the matched condition.
For both GLMMs, statistical significance was assessed using conventional NHST and a threshold of alpha < 0.05.

In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants achieved an overall accuracy of 91% when pooling all trials together (including trials with neutral expressions only).
Error analysis revealed that misses accounted for 8.1% of responses, while false alarms constituted 0.9%.
When looking at each emotion individually, detection accuracy was on average lower for angry (~81%) than for happy faces (~98%; Figure 2a).

Angry versus happy RMSD was substantially higher in the unmatched-intensity condition (M = 0.55 ± 0.01) than in the matchedintensity condition (M = 0.20 ± 0.18).

text.text: Furthermore, we verified that any observed differences between conditions were not confounded by participant characteristics, and thus confirmed that the two cohorts were demographically balanced.
Fisher's exact test showed no significant difference in gender distribution between groups (p = .511).
Similarly, a Wilcoxon rank-sum test found no significant differences in age (p = .569), and laterality quotient (LQ) was comparable across groups (p = .680).

Chi-square tests yielded no significant association between gender and handedness within either group (unmatched-intensity condition: χ² = .636, p = .727; matched-intensity condition: χ² = 3.476, p = .176).

Additionally, we conducted a k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification analysis by incorporating participants' gender, age, and laterality quotient (LQ) into the feature set alongside behavioral measures (i.e., accuracy and response time).
Separate models were trained for the unmatched-and matched-intensity conditions.

In the unmatched-intensity condition, the inclusion of these additional variables did not significantly affect classification accuracy, which remained at 67.9% (bootstrapped 95% CI: 67.3% -68.6%), comparable to the 68.4% accuracy observed with behavioral features alone.
Similarly, in the matched-intensity condition, the extended model achieved an accuracy of 51.5% (bootstrapped 95% CI: 50.8% -52.2%), supporting H 0 .

Feature importance analysis confirmed that in the unmatched-intensity condition, detection speed was the most influential predictor, with a substantial decrease in model accuracy when permuted (10.5% ± 0.47%).
Response accuracy had a small effect (1.59% ± 0.28%), while demographic variables, such as age, gender, and laterality quotient, had minimal impact (0.03%, 0.01%, and 0.15%, respectively).

In the matched-intensity condition, all predictors contributed less to classification: permutation of RTs led to a 1.37% ± 0.27% drop in accuracy, response accuracy resulted in a 0.42% ± 0.32% decline, and demographic variables again showed negligible influence (0.40%, 0.02%, and 0.27%, respectively).
These findings indicate that demographic factors and handedness are irrelevant for classifying detected facial expressions from behavioral performance.

text.text: A second preregistered experiment with a within-subject design was conducted to test the replicability of findings obtained in Study 1.
The present study employed a within-subject design to replicate the effect observed in the preregistered matched-intensity condition from Study 1.

To this end, individuals who had previously participated in the unmatched-intensity condition (where angry and happy faces were displayed at their maximum, unequalized intensity) were re-invited to complete the matchedintensity condition.
Consistent with the original study protocol, facial expressions in the matchedintensity condition were presented at an intermediate, perceptually-equalized intensity level across emotions.
This follow-up was preregistered as an update to the original study registration and is publicly accessible at http://osf.io/sjvak.
text.formatted: This follow-up was preregistered as an update to the original study registration and is publicly accessible at <ref type="url" target="http://osf.io/sjvak">osf.io/sjvak</ref>.

text.text: The conduction of Study 2 was motivated by both theoretical and statistical considerations.

Testing for the presence or absence of the HSE within the same participants potentially reduces error variance attributable to inter-individual differences (e.g., perceptual sensitivity, attentional strategies, or baseline emotion detection ability), thereby allowing more robust inferences regarding the role of low-level visual features.

Consequently, any observed effects (or lack thereof) can be more confidently attributed to the experimental manipulation (i.e., intensity matching of facial expressions) rather than to uncontrolled betweenparticipant variability.
For a visual depiction of the experimental design from both Studies 1 and 2, see the OSF project repository at http://osf.io/vhcyt.
text.formatted: For a visual depiction of the experimental design from both Studies 1 and 2, see the OSF project repository at <ref type="url" target="http://osf.io/vhcyt">osf.io/vhcyt</ref>.

text.text: To replicate the absence of the HSE observed in the matched-intensity condition, individuals who had previously completed the unmatched-intensity condition were re-invited to participate in the follow-up study.
Recruitment was conducted using the "Include List" feature on the Prolific platform, which facilitated the precise identification and targeted re-invitation of eligible individuals.

Data collection for Study 2 began at least two weeks after the completion of the initial session, allowing for a sufficient washout period to minimize potential carryover effects related to stimuli memorization.
All participants received the link to the experiment as in the previous session but were directed to complete the matched-intensity condition task.
The order of condition exposure was therefore fixed: all participants first completed the unmatched-intensity task and were subsequently invited to complete the matched-intensity one.
The maximum data collection period was set at two weeks; however, data collection could conclude earlier if all eligible participants completed the task before the deadline.
Notably, participants received compensation consistent with that of Study 1.

In accordance with the original preregistered protocol, the target sample size for Study 2 was set at 115 participants, each completing 250 trials in the matched-intensity condition (50 trials per block across 5 blocks).
As specified in the preregistration update, if fewer than 115 participants completed Study 2, additional participants with no prior involvement in any of our experiments would be recruited.
These new participants were asked to complete both the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions in that fixed order, separated by a washout period of at least two weeks.

Since the target sample size was not reached within the initial cohort (n = 80), recruitment was extended to include an additional 70 newly enrolled participants, who were asked to take part in both experimental sessions.
They first undertook the unmatched-intensity condition and, after a two-week washout period, were recontacted to engage in the matched-intensity condition.
Of these, 60 returned for the second session (drop-out rate = ~14%).
As the study design required within-participants comparisons, analyses were restricted to those participants who completed both conditions.
This resulted in a total of 140 participants (80 from the first wave and 60 from the second) eligible for inclusion.
Accordingly, a matched subset of 140 participants was extracted from the unmatched-intensity dataset: specifically, those who also completed the matchedintensity condition.
Following this procedure, the final pre-exclusion sample consisted of 140 participants for each condition.
Data quality control was then applied following the same exclusion criteria as in Study 1.
No participants were excluded based on completion times below the first quartile (Q1) minus 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR).

However, participants whose accuracy in either emotion category fell below Q1 -1.5 × IQR were removed to mitigate the influence of random responses, inattentiveness, or misunderstanding of task instructions.

This led to the exclusion of 17 participants in the unmatched-intensity condition and 11 in the matched-intensity condition, with overlapping exclusions resulting in a final sample of 115 participants retained for analysis.
Therefore, no random subsampling was required and the final sample comprised all eligible participants who completed both sessions and passed exclusion criteria.
At the trial level, responses with reaction times exceeding Q3 + 1.5 × IQR were removed, as such latencies may indicate distraction or disengagement.
This resulted in the exclusion of 1,098 trials from the unmatchedintensity condition and 1,323 trials from the matched-intensity condition.
The experimental procedure for Study 2 largely followed the protocol of Study 1, involving the same visual search task and trial structure.
Participants who had previously completed the unmatched-intensity condition were invited to complete the matched-intensity condition only.

For participants newly recruited during Study 2, both the unmatched-intensity and matched-intensity conditions were administered sequentially, with a washout period of at least two weeks between sessions.
Detailed descriptions of the task design, instructions, and stimuli presentation are provided in the Study 1 Methods section.
For Study 2, we replicated the analysis pipeline used in the original preregistered study.

Specifically, the same code and functions uploaded to the OSF project repository prior to the preregistration update were applied to the Study 2 dataset, ensuring consistency in all analyses across studies.
This includes variable transformations, inference criteria, data exclusion rules, treatment of missing data, and exploratory analyses.
A central aim of the present study was to test whether detection performance is better accounted for by perceptual features than by emotional categorization.

Therefore, in addition to all previously described analyses, we measured whether participants responded more accurately and faster to faces that are perceptually more distinctive, irrespective of the emotion they depict.

First of all, we quantified the magnitude of facial displacement of angry and happy expressions with respect to a neutral configuration and tested whether larger deviations systematically predicted more accurate and faster responses.

For each stimulus, we computed the root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) between the actor's reconstructed 3D facial mesh of the neutral frame (Frame 1) and that of the frames selected to represent each emotional expression.

In the unmatched-intensity condition, the apex frames from angry and happy video sequences were identified through framewise displacement analysis; in the matched-intensity condition, the frames were selected during the intensity-matching task (see Study 1: Stimulus selection and perceptual matching for details).
As expected, a Wilcoxon rank-sum test confirmed that RMSD values were significantly greater in the unmatched than in the matched-intensity condition (z = 2.37, p = .018).
We then evaluated whether this geometric distance explained response accuracy and RTs at the stimulus level.

Data from all experimental designs were pooled and aggregated into actor × emotion × condition units, so that for each unique combination we computed (a) the proportion of correct responses (accuracy) across all emotionaltarget trials and (b) the mean RT across correctly-detected trials, along with the stimulus's corresponding geometric deviation from the neutral baseline.
This procedure yielded 76 stimuluslevel observations.
The aggregated data were analyzed using two Generalized Linear Mixedeffects Models (GLMMs) predicting detection performance from geometric deviation, condition, and their interaction.

In both models, condition was included to reflect systematic differences in deformation magnitude arising from the stimulus-construction procedure, and the interaction term assessed whether the influence of geometric deviation differed between unmatched-and matchedintensity conditions.
Emotion was added to determine whether categorical emotion explained variance in accuracy and RTs beyond geometric structure.
Actor identity was included as a random intercept to account for between-actor variability: [accuracy OR RTs] ~ geometric distance * condition + emotion + (1|actor_ID)

text.text: Visual search performance was assessed using the same behavioral metrics as in Study 1: detection accuracy and response latency.
In the unmatched-intensity condition, participants achieved an overall accuracy of ~90% when aggregating trials across emotional categories (including trials with neutral expressions only).
Error analysis revealed that misses accounted for 9.1% of responses, while false alarm represented 1.1%.
When looking at each emotion individually, angry targets were detected with an average accuracy of ~79%, whereas happy targets were identified with ~97% accuracy.
In contrast, overall performance declined in the matchedintensity condition, dropping to 85.3%, with misses representing the 12.9% of errors and false alarms the 1.8%.
In this condition, the disparity in detection accuracy between emotional categories was attenuated: angry targets were detected with an accuracy of 84%, and happy expressions with 82% accuracy.
Reaction times (RTs) mirrored these patterns.

In the unmatchedintensity condition, angry targets were accurately detected with an average RT of 1,769 ± 765 milliseconds, whereas happy targets were correctly identified more rapidly, with a mean RT of 1,278 ± 519 milliseconds.
In the matched-intensity condition, detection latencies increased overall, with angry expressions detected at a mean RT of 1,799 ± 809 milliseconds and happy expressions at 1,732 ± 855 milliseconds.

The same k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) classification procedure used in Study 1 was applied to Study 2, with separate models trained on data from the unmatched-and matchedintensity conditions to predict emotional expression (happy vs. angry) based on participants' reaction times (RTs) and accuracy.
In the unmatched-intensity condition, the model achieved an average classification accuracy of 68.7%.
The bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for this estimate ranged from 68.1% to 69.3%, exceeding the predefined SESOI of 66%.
By contrast, classification performance in the matched-intensity condition yielded an average test accuracy of 53.5%, with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval ranging from 52.8% to 54.2%.

Again, the upper bound of this interval fell well below the SESOI threshold of 66%, indicating that behavioral features no longer carried practically meaningful information for emotion prediction when facial expression intensity was equalized.

Feature importance analysis showed that, in the unmatchedintensity condition, detection speed had a dominant influence on classification (9.53% ± 0.01% drop in model accuracy when permuted), whereas response accuracy contributed modestly, with a 1.67% ± 0.36% decrease.
In the matched-intensity condition, both features were less informative: RTs led to a 3.18% ± 0.42% drop, and accuracy contributed only 1.18% ± 0.37%.
In addition, we conducted a non-preregistered single-subject k-NN classification analysis on data merged from both experimental designs.
In the unmatched-intensity condition, the average classification accuracy reached 67.9%, with a 95% bootstrapped confidence interval ranging from 66.3% to 69.5%.
In contrast, in the matched-intensity condition the average classification accuracy was 54.1%, with a 95% confidence interval of 53.0% to 55.2%.

As the entire confidence interval lies above the SESOI in the case of the unmatched-intensity condition and below it in the case of matched-intensity condition, these additional analyses confirm support for the presence (H 1 ) of the HSE when perceptual features are not controlled and its absence (H 0 ) when, instead, perceptual features are equalized.

Consistent with the approach adopted in Study 1, we conducted exploratory analyses using Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMMs) to assess the influence of emotional expression, intensity condition, and their interaction on visual search performance.
A GLMM with a binomial distribution and logit link function was applied to response accuracy data (n = 41,951 observations in total).

The model included fixed effects for emotion expression, intensity condition, and their interaction, and random intercepts for participants (participant_id), stimuli (actor_id), and laterality quotient (lq).
The analysis yielded a significant main effect of emotion, with higher accuracy for happy rather than angry faces (B = 2.410, 95% CI [2.283, 2.538], SE = .065, t = 37.02, p < .001).

text.text: A significant main effect of the experimental condition was also observed, indicating higher accuracy in the matched-intensity condition compared to the unmatched-intensity condition (B = .409, 95% CI [.333, .484], SE = .039, t = 10.60, p < .001).

text.text: Importantly, the interaction between emotion and condition was also significant (B = -2.611, 95% CI [-2.760, -2.461], SE = .076, t = -34.25, p < .001), indicating that the accuracy advantage for happy faces was markedly attenuated when expression intensity was matched.

text.text: A separate GLMM with an inverse Gaussian distribution and log link function was estimated to model RTs, employing the same fixed-and random-effects structure as the accuracy model.
Following the exclusion of incorrect responses, 35,866 trials were retained in total.
The model revealed a significant main effect of emotion, with faster detection of happy faces relative to angry faces (B = -.317, 95% CI [-.329, -.305], SE = .006, t = -51.40, p < .001).

text.text: In this model, the main effect of intensity condition was not statistically significant (B = -.004, 95% CI [-.017, .010], SE = .007, t = -.53, p = .599).

However, the interaction between emotion and condition did reach significance (B = .280, 95% CI [.263, .298], SE = .009, t = 30.92, p < .001), suggesting that the detection speed advantage for happy faces was attenuated under the matched-intensity condition, where perceptual features were equated.
